explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The man says, "Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me." (Luke 12:13) He wants Jesus to step in on a family money matter. Notice he asks it out loud, right in front of the whole crowd.

explanations.answer: Pay back what you borrowed from me
explanations.explanation: Close to a real family fight, but this one isn't a loan. Nothing in the text says the brother borrowed a thing. The man asks Jesus to tell his brother "to divide the inheritance with me." (Luke 12:13) It's about an inheritance, not a debt.

explanations.answer: Give back the field you took from me
explanations.explanation: I can see why a field might come to mind, since inheritances can include land. But the text never mentions a field or anything being taken. The man says, "Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me." (Luke 12:13) That's the whole request.
Not this time, friend. Jesus doesn't take the case. He says, "Man, who appointed Me judge or executor between you?" (Luke 12:14) That's a question, and it isn't a yes.

Right, baker. Jesus doesn't agree to settle it. He answers, "Man, who appointed Me judge or executor between you?" (Luke 12:14) Then He moves on to something bigger, which is how this whole teaching gets started.
Yes, greed. Jesus says, "Watch out! Guard yourselves against every form of greed…" (Luke 12:15) Look at that word "every." He isn't picking out one kind. He means all of them.

Fear is a fair guess, since people worry about money all the time. But that's not the word Jesus uses here. He says, "Guard yourselves against every form of greed…" (Luke 12:15) The warning is about wanting more, not being afraid.
Pride is a sneaky one, and I've had my own moments with it. But Jesus doesn't say pride here. He says, "Guard yourselves against every form of greed…" (Luke 12:15) That's the word to hold onto.

explanations.answer: Life is not about how much you own
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, "…for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions." (Luke 12:15) You can own a LOT and that still isn't what your life is made of. It's the reason behind the warning.

explanations.answer: Riches can be stolen in a moment
explanations.explanation: Plenty of people worry about that, but it's not the reason Jesus gives. He says, "…one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions." (Luke 12:15) His point is about what life consists of. He doesn't mention theft.

explanations.answer: Money always splits up a family
explanations.explanation: The man's request does come from a family dispute, so I get the guess. But Jesus never says money always does that. His reason is, "…one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions." (Luke 12:15)

Yep, store. The rich man thinks, "What shall I do, since I have nowhere to store my crops?" (Luke 12:17) The ground gave him an abundance, and now he's out of room. That's a problem I would LOVE to have.
Selling is a smart thought, but it's not what the man says. He thinks, "What shall I do, since I have nowhere to store my crops?" (Luke 12:17) His trouble is room, so the word is store.
Planting comes before a harvest, not after. By this point the ground has already "produced an abundance." (Luke 12:16) The man's worry is, "I have nowhere to store my crops." (Luke 12:17)

explanations.answer: Tear down his barns and will build bigger ones
explanations.explanation: That's the plan, baker. He says, "I will tear down my barns and will build bigger ones, and there I will store up all my grain and my goods." (Luke 12:18) Notice who he's talking to. It's all "I will" and "my."

explanations.answer: Sell all of it before it can spoil
explanations.explanation: That would be a plan, but it's not his. The text never mentions spoiling or selling. He says, "I will tear down my barns and will build bigger ones…" (Luke 12:18) He wants more room to keep it all.

explanations.answer: Give the extra away to his neighbors
explanations.explanation: That would be a very different story, friend. But he never thinks about neighbors. He says, "I will tear down my barns and will build bigger ones, and there I will store up all my grain and my goods." (Luke 12:18)

True, baker. He plans to say to himself, "You have plenty of good things laid up for many years." (Luke 12:19) That's quite a pep talk, and he's the only one in the audience. I bet it felt great while it lasted.

It's true, friend. The man says, "Then I will say to myself, 'You have plenty of good things laid up for many years…'" (Luke 12:19) He fully plans to say it. The speech is all in his head, and God hasn't weighed in yet.

explanations.answer: His life will be required of him
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. God says, "This very night your life will be required of you." (Luke 12:20) Look at that timing. He planned for many years, and God speaks about tonight.

explanations.answer: His barns will be burned with fire
explanations.explanation: Nope, no fire in this parable. God says, "This very night your life will be required of you." (Luke 12:20) The barns aren't what God talks about. He talks about the man's life.

explanations.answer: His grain will be taken by thieves
explanations.explanation: Thieves are a natural guess, but they never show up. God says, "This very night your life will be required of you." (Luke 12:20) The warning is about the man himself, not his grain.
True, baker. God says, "Then who will own what you have accumulated?" (Luke 12:20) It's a question, and the man gets no answer in the text. All those barns, and nobody named to get them.
It's true, friend. God does ask. He says, "Then who will own what you have accumulated?" (Luke 12:20) The man planned for many years of good living. That question comes right after "This very night."
Yes, God. Jesus says, "This is how it will be for anyone who stores up treasure for himself but is not rich toward God." (Luke 12:21) That's the one thing the man left out. Good work, baker.
Giving to others is a good thing, but it's not the word here. Jesus says, "…anyone who stores up treasure for himself but is not rich toward God." (Luke 12:21) The word is God.

Family matters a lot, and this whole teaching started with two brothers. But Jesus doesn't say family here. He says, "…anyone who stores up treasure for himself but is not rich toward God." (Luke 12:21)
